title: Joseph Dies, and Egypt Turns
sum: After Jacob's death Israel grows into a great nation, and while Joseph lives there is "no satan and nothing evil" (46:2). Joseph dies at 110, and the angel adds what Genesis leaves out: why his bones stayed in Egypt. A Canaanite king, Makamaron, kills the king of Egypt, and the border is shut, so Egypt will not carry another body to Canaan. Years later, in another war, the Israelites take the bones of Jacob's other sons to the double cave at Hebron, and some of them, Moses' father Amram among them, stay behind.

Then the story turns to Exodus 1. The king of Canaan defeats Egypt, and the new Pharaoh fears that Israel, whose "hearts and faces are turned toward the land of Canaan," will side with the enemy. Forced labor begins, Pithom and Rameses are built, and Israel keeps growing.
readings: Read as a bridge

The chapter closes Genesis and opens Exodus in one movement. Jubilees fills the gap between Genesis 50 and Exodus 1 with a war, and so explains three things the Bible leaves open: why Joseph's bones waited (Exodus 13:19), where the brothers were buried, and why a new king feared Israel.
Read as a lesson

The order of the chapter is a moral. While the brothers love one another and Joseph lives, no evil touches them (46:1-2). Once that generation is gone, oppression begins. The same pattern, faithfulness bringing peace and its loss bringing harm, runs through the whole book (23:26-29; 50:5).

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox churches this chapter is part of the revelation given to Moses, read beside the end of Genesis and the start of Exodus in the Orit. It explains, from Moses' own book of divisions, how Israel came to be enslaved.
views.H: Historical critics see a writer filling the gap between Genesis and Exodus. Charles 1902 thought the war of Egypt and Canaan was the oldest form of a legend later told in many versions, and that it points to a time when Egypt had lost its hold on Syria.
views.N: The burial of the patriarchs stands behind Stephen's words that "our ancestors" were moved to a tomb in Canaan (Acts 7:15-16), and Joseph's bones behind Hebrews 11:22. Charles thought Stephen used a tradition like this one, though Stephen names Shechem.
views.J: Josephus also has the brothers buried at Hebron, and so does a related work, the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs (Charles 1902).
views.W: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers can take the chapter as an early Jewish answer to questions Genesis and Exodus raise, not as added history. Its war and its kings have no support outside Jubilees and works that depend on it.

echoes: Genesis 50:22-26; Exodus 1:1-14; Exodus 13:19; Acts 7:15-18; Hebrews 11:22; Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs

settings.what: The angel's account of Joseph's death and the start of the oppression
settings.by: the angel of the presence, dictating on Mount Sinai (1:27-2:1)
settings.to: Moses on Mount Sinai, in the first year after the Exodus, and through him all Israel
settings.when: after the Exodus, as Moses hears the story of his own people's past
settings.why: To show Moses why Joseph's bones were still in Egypt for him to carry (46:5; Exodus 13:19) and why Egypt turned on Israel: not by chance, but after a war and out of fear that Israel belonged to Canaan.
settings.readers: Jews in the land of Israel in the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card), for whom the land of Canaan was the heart of the matter: the book tells them their fathers' faces were always "turned toward the land of Canaan" (46:13), and that even in Egypt some stayed in Hebron (46:10).

settings.when: after Egypt's defeat by the king of Canaan (46:11)
settings.why: To win his people over to forced labor by playing on their fear of war and of a people whose loyalty lay elsewhere. It follows Exodus 1:9-10.
settings.readers: Readers who knew Exodus 1 hear its words with a new reason added: Israel's longing for its land.

title: Moses Is Born
sum: The angel now speaks of Moses himself. His father Amram returns from Canaan, and Moses is born in the year 2330 by the book's count, in the time of Pharaoh's order to drown the boys. The story follows Exodus 2 closely but fills in names and details: his mother hides him three months until someone reports her, leaves him in the ark for seven days, nurses him by night while Miriam guards him from birds by day. Pharaoh's daughter, here named Tarmut, finds him and takes pity.

Two changes stand out. Moses' father Amram teaches him writing, and Moses spends three weeks of years, twenty-one years, at court. At forty-two he kills an Egyptian who was beating an Israelite and flees when another Israelite asks, "Who put you as a chief and a judge over us?"
readings: Read with Exodus

Almost every line has a source in Exodus 2, and Jubilees adds names from later chapters: Jochebed and Amram (Exodus 6:20), Miriam (Exodus 15:20; Numbers 26:59). It is a careful reader's retelling, smoothing the text and answering its small questions.
Read as a portrait

The changes shape a picture of Moses. He is taught by his Hebrew father, not by Egypt's wise men; his killing of the Egyptian is told without blame; and he flees not from Pharaoh but at an Israelite's words. The next chapter shows that his real enemy is Mastema.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox churches this is the angel's own telling of Moses' birth, read with Exodus 2. It names the women of the story, Tarmut, Jochebed and Miriam.
views.H: Scholars note how Jubilees supplies names and dates, as later midrash would. Charles 1902 traced several details: Tarmut matches Josephus' Thermouthis, and the "Hebrew women" of 47:5 may be a translator's slip.
views.N: Acts 7:20-29 retells the same story with a different emphasis: Moses "was schooled in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" and was about forty. Hebrews 11:23-27 praises the faith of his parents and of Moses himself.
views.J: Josephus and later Jewish writers also name Pharaoh's daughter and fill in Moses' childhood. Jubilees is one of the earliest witnesses to that habit.
views.W: Most churches read this as an early Jewish retelling of Exodus 2. Its details are not history in addition to the Bible, but they show how Jews before Christ read the story.

settings.what: The angel tells Moses the story of his own birth and youth
settings.by: the angel of the presence, dictating on Mount Sinai (1:27-2:1)
settings.when: on Mount Sinai, in the year 2410 by the book's count (50:4), eighty years after Moses' birth (47:1)
settings.why: To remind Moses that his life was guarded and his learning came from his own father, so that he receives the law as one of Israel's line of faithful men, not as a man of Egypt.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card), who are shown a Moses taught to write by a Hebrew father rather than by a foreign culture (compare Acts 7:22).

title: Mastema Against Moses
sum: Moses lives away from Egypt (in Midian, as the Latin says) and, by the book's dates, comes back at eighty. On the road, Prince Mastema tries to kill him, to keep the Egyptians safe, and the angel of the presence rescues him. This is Jubilees' version of Exodus 4:24, where "the LORD met him and sought to kill him." Then the angel sums up the ten plagues and Mastema's help to Pharaoh's sorcerers: the angels let them cause harm but never heal.

At the sea, the angel stands between the camps. Mastema is bound from the fourteenth to the eighteenth of the first month, so that he cannot accuse Israel while they take Egypt's silver and gold as back pay, then he is let loose so the Egyptians will pursue to their ruin. A thousand Egyptians die for every Hebrew baby drowned in the river.
readings: Read as a war in heaven

Behind the Exodus stands a struggle between the angel of the presence and Prince Mastema. Every scene of Exodus 4-14 has its unseen side: the attack on the road, the magicians' power, the hardening of hearts, the pursuit. Yet Mastema acts only as far as God allows, and is bound and loosed at God's command.
Read as an answer to hard verses

The chapter answers questions Exodus raises. Why would God try to kill Moses (Exodus 4:24)? Jubilees: it was Mastema. Was the plunder of Egypt theft (Exodus 12:36)? Jubilees: it was back pay, and the accuser was bound. Why did the magicians succeed at first? Jubilees: Mastema helped them.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox churches the chapter reveals the spiritual battle behind the Exodus, in which God's angel guards Moses and the evil one is bound. It is read with Exodus 4-14.
views.H: Charles 1902 saw the author doing what the Chronicler did in 1 Chronicles 21:1: moving a troubling act from God to an evil spirit (here Exodus 4:24 and 14:8). Scholars see a growing belief in a leader of evil spirits in the centuries before Christ.
views.N: The chapter shows ideas the New Testament shares: an accuser of God's people (Revelation 12:10), an evil leader bound and later loosed (Revelation 20:2-3), magicians who "stood against Moses" (2 Timothy 3:8), and the destroyer at the Exodus (1 Corinthians 10:10; Hebrews 11:28).
views.J: Later Jewish tradition also explained Exodus 4:24 by an angel (Charles cites Targum Pseudo-Jonathan) and named the magicians. The Mekhilta has the Egyptians pursue from the nineteenth, as here (Charles, citing Beer).
views.W: Most churches value the chapter as background to the New Testament's language about the devil, but the Bible itself says the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart and met Moses on the road. Readers are invited to hold both: God rules, and evil powers act only within his will (compare Job 1-2).

deep.h: Who did it? God and Mastema in the Exodus
deep.b:
Four times Jubilees gives Mastema, or his powers, a deed that Exodus gives to God:

EventExodusJubilees
The attack on the road"the LORD met him and sought to kill him" (Exodus 4:24)Prince Mastema wanted to kill Moses (48:2-3)
The magicians' signsthey "did the same with their spells" (Exodus 7:22)Mastema helped them (48:9)
The hardening at the sea"The LORD made the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt stubborn" (Exodus 14:8)"He hardened their hearts" (Charles reads "he" as Mastema, loosed in 48:16), yet the Egyptians "were made bold by the Lord our God" (48:16-17)
The firstborn"the LORD struck every firstborn" (Exodus 12:29)"all the powers of Mastema were sent out" (49:2)

The same move appears earlier, when Mastema, not God, proposes Abraham's test (17:16; compare Genesis 22:1). The Bible itself does this once: 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD stirred David up, and 1 Chronicles 21:1 says "Satan stood up against Israel." Jubilees never lets Mastema act on his own: he is bound and loosed by the angels, and his powers are "sent."

echoes: Exodus 4:19-26; Exodus 7-14; Genesis 15:13-14; 2 Timothy 3:8; Revelation 12:10; Revelation 20:2-3; Wisdom of Solomon 18:5; 1 Chronicles 21:1

settings.what: The angel recalls Moses' return, the plagues and the sea
settings.by: the angel of the presence, dictating on Mount Sinai (1:27-2:1)
settings.to: Moses, who lived through these events ("You yourself know," 48:2)
settings.when: at Sinai, soon after the crossing of the sea
settings.why: To show Moses the unseen side of what he saw: the angel's rescue, Mastema's opposition, and the binding of the accuser so that Israel's taking of Egypt's goods was just. It assures him that God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15:14) was kept to the letter.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card) who knew the hard verses of Exodus and faced foreign rulers; the book tells them that behind every oppressor stands a spirit God can bind.

title: The Law of the Passover
sum: The angel turns from story to law. The Passover must be kept every year on its day: the lamb slaughtered on the fourteenth of the first month, at the edge of evening, and eaten that night, the start of the fifteenth, until the third part of the night. On the night in Egypt, "all the powers of Mastema" were sent to kill Egypt's firstborn, and they passed over every house marked with blood while Israel ate, drank wine and praised God.

The law is engraved on the heavenly tablets. The lamb is roasted, never boiled; no bone may be broken, "for no bone of the Israelites will be crushed." Once Israel is in the land, it may be eaten only before the Lord's tabernacle, and later only in the courtyard of the sanctuary, by men twenty and older. The chapter ends with the seven days of unleavened bread, first kept on the march from Egypt to the shore of the sea.
readings: Read as law

The chapter gathers the Passover rules of Exodus 12, Numbers 9 and Deuteronomy 16 into one law and settles questions they leave open: the exact hours of "between the evenings," when the meal must end, where it may be eaten, and who must eat it. On each point it takes the stricter side, and it ties the date to the heavenly tablets so that it can never move.
Read as story and hope

The Passover remembers a night of rescue: the destroying powers passed over Israel. Jubilees promises that each year it is rightly kept, "no plague will come on them" (49:15). Christians read the unbroken bones and the lamb's blood in the light of John 19:36 and 1 Corinthians 5:7.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox churches the chapter is part of the law revealed to Moses. Christians read the Passover lamb as pointing to Christ, "our Passover" (1 Corinthians 5:7), whose bones were not broken (John 19:36).
views.H: Scholars note how strongly the chapter ties the Passover to one sanctuary and to fixed hours, and how it differs from later rabbinic practice on the hour of slaughter, the end of the meal and the age of those who must come (Charles 1902). These were live questions among priests in the 100s BC.
views.N: Jesus' last Passover meal, with its cup (Luke 22:17-20), John's "No bone of his will be broken" (John 19:36), and "the one who destroyed the firstborn" (Hebrews 11:28) all gain background here. Luke 2:41-42 shows a family going up to Jerusalem for the feast, as this law requires.
views.J: Jewish practice later followed the rabbis rather than Jubilees: the meal could be eaten anywhere in Jerusalem and finished by midnight (Charles 1902). After AD 70, with no temple, the lamb was no longer sacrificed. Jubilees' mention of wine is among the oldest for the Passover meal.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as a witness to how the Passover was kept in the time between the Testaments, and as background to the Lord's Supper, without treating its added rules as binding.

echoes: Exodus 12:1-51; Numbers 9:1-14; Numbers 28:16-25; Deuteronomy 16:1-8; Leviticus 23:5-8; 2 Chronicles 35:1-19; John 19:36; 1 Corinthians 5:7; Hebrews 11:28; Luke 22:7-20

settings.what: The law of the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread
settings.by: the angel of the presence, giving the law as written on the heavenly tablets
settings.to: Moses, who is to command all Israel (49:15; 49:22)
settings.when: at Sinai, in the first year after the Exodus, looking ahead to the tabernacle in the land and the later temple (49:18-19)
settings.why: It binds every clean Israelite man, twenty and older (49:9; 49:17), once a year on the fourteenth of the first month, first at the tabernacle and then at the temple only. It answers the danger of a moved or neglected feast: kept on the wrong day or in the wrong place, the Passover loses its protection (49:15).
settings.readers: Jews in the land of Israel in the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card), when the Passover was kept at the Jerusalem temple. The book's 364-day year (6:32) made the date fixed, and its rule on the hour touches a question on which, Charles 1902 notes, the Pharisees and the Sadducees differed (49:10-12).
views: The repeated "do not move it" (49:7; 49:14) may be aimed at a calendar that let the feasts drift, such as a moon-based year (compare 6:36-38).
The details of blood, fat, courtyard and hours read like instructions for priests at the temple.

title: Jubilees and Sabbaths
sum: The book ends with time itself. The angel recalls the Sabbath laws first given in the Wilderness of Sin and the laws for the Sabbath years and jubilees given on Sinai, and sums up history: forty-nine jubilees from Adam to this day, plus a week of years and two years. Forty more years in the wilderness will bring Israel into Canaan, exactly at the end of fifty jubilees, and the jubilees will go on until Israel is clean and there is "no satan" in the land.

Then the Sabbath law: six days of work and the seventh for the Lord. The penalty for working is death, and the list is long: travel, buying and selling, drawing water not prepared the day before, carrying loads, lying with one's wife, plowing, lighting a fire, riding, sailing, hunting, killing, fasting and making war. Only the sanctuary's offerings may be made. The Sabbath is a day for eating, drinking and blessing God, "a day of the holy kingdom for all Israel." A last line closes "the account of the division of the days."
readings: Read as the book's goal

Jubilees began with the Sabbath at creation (2:17-33) and ends with it. Its whole dating system, weeks of years and jubilees, is the Sabbath principle stretched over history. The fifty jubilees from Adam to the Jordan make Israel's entry into the land a great Jubilee, a return home.
Read as strict law

The list of Sabbath crimes is stricter than the Bible's and stricter than later rabbinic law in places (marital relations, war), though milder in others. Charles 1902 read it against the persecution of the Maccabean era, when keeping the Sabbath could cost one's life (1 Maccabees 2:29-41).

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox churches this is the close of the law revealed to Moses. Christian readers in those churches read its strict rules through the New Testament's teaching on the Sabbath.
views.H: Historical critics use 50:12 to date the book: a ban on all fighting on the Sabbath fits the time before Mattathias allowed defensive war (1 Maccabees 2:41), or a protest against it. Charles 1902 notes that the ban on all warfare was observed literally before and during the outbreak of the Maccabean wars, until Mattathias allowed defense.
views.N: The chapter shows how strict some Jews were about the Sabbath in Jesus' time. Jesus' answers stand in sharp contrast: "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings, and not human beings for the sake of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27), and the priests' temple work (Matthew 12:5), which 50:10-11 also allows.
views.J: Some of these rules (no travel beyond a limit, no carrying, no fire, no fasting) became rabbinic law in milder form; others (no marital relations) were rejected by the Mishnah but kept by the Samaritans, Karaites and Beta Israel (Charles 1902).
views.W: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers do not take these laws as binding. For how the churches differ on the Sabbath and Sunday, see the card at Exodus 20 and the cards at Colossians 2 and Galatians 4.

echoes: Exodus 16:22-30; Exodus 20:8-11; Exodus 31:12-17; Exodus 35:1-3; Leviticus 25:1-12; Numbers 15:32-36; Jeremiah 17:21-22; Nehemiah 13:15-22; 1 Maccabees 2:29-41; Mark 2:23-28; Matthew 12:1-14

The Sabbath debates of the Gospels (Mark 2:23-3:6; Luke 13:10-17; John 5:1-18) took place among Jews who knew rules like these. For the churches' answers on keeping the Sabbath, see the card at Exodus 20.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the book ends at the edge of the land
deep.b: Jubilees stops at Sinai, forty years and one jubilee short of the Jordan (50:4). By ending with the land's Sabbaths (50:2-3) and the Jubilee still to come, the book leaves its readers where Moses stood: holding the law, waiting to enter. For Jews in the 100s BC, who lived in the land but under foreign rule, that may have been the point. The fiftieth jubilee is promised, but Israel must first be "made clean" (50:5). This reading is Claude's; it overlaps with scholars who see the book's dates as a scheme pointing to Israel's future.

settings.what: The law of the land's Sabbaths and the count of the jubilees
settings.to: Moses on Mount Sinai, for Israel about to enter the land
settings.when: in the year 2410 from creation by the book's count, forty years before the crossing of the Jordan
settings.why: It binds Israel once it is in the land, where the land itself must keep its Sabbath years and jubilees (Leviticus 25). It answers the question of when the count begins: not until Israel enters (50:2).
settings.readers: Jews living in the land in the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card), for whom Sabbath years were a real economic matter (1 Maccabees 6:49 and 6:53 mention one) and whose history the book frames as jubilees moving toward a cleansed Israel.

settings.what: The Sabbath law with its penalties
settings.by: the angel of the presence, writing from the tablets God gave him (50:13)
settings.to: Moses, for every Israelite, slave, animal and foreigner in Israel (50:7)
settings.when: at Sinai, as the last word of the book
settings.why: It binds every household in Israel, at home and "in any place" (50:12), every seventh day, with death as the penalty. It answers the problem of a Sabbath kept loosely: the list spells out what counts as work, and allows only the sanctuary's sacrifices.
settings.readers: Charles 1902 read the ban on war (50:12) against the early Maccabean years, when loyal Jews died rather than fight on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:38); the strict rule on marriage he linked to the same hard times. The law was kept in part by later strict groups, among them the Beta Israel of Ethiopia.
views: Read as written before 1 Maccabees 2:41, the law records the view of those who died in the caves.
Read as written after it, the law is a protest against the new permission to fight in self-defense.
